## HARVARD SCHOOL OF PUBLIC HEALTH

## Occupational Asthma and Contact Dermatitis in a Spray Painter after Introduction of an Aziridine Cross-Linker

Christopher T. Leffler and Donald K. Milton

Occupational Health Program, Department of Environmental Health, Harvard School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

A 23-year-old spray developed contact dermatitis and respiratory difficulty characterized by small airways obstruction shortly after the polyfunctional aziridine cross-linker CX-10O to be used in his workplace as activator. The symptoms resolved after he was removed from the workplace and was treated with inhaled and steroids. Painters may have an increased risk of asthma due to exposure to variety of agents, such as isocyanates, alkyd resins, and chromates. This case illustrates the importance of appropriate work practices and personal protective equipment to minimize exposure. Occupational asthma is diagnosed by a histo ry of work-related symptoms and exposure to known causative agents. The diagnosis is confirmed by serial pulmonary function Or inhalational challenge The risk of asthma attributable to occupational exposures is probably underappreciated due to underreporting and to inappropriate use of narrow definitions of exposure in epidemiologic studes of attributable risk. words: aziridine, contact dermatitis, occupational asthma, personal protective equipment, spray painting: Environ Health Perspect 107.599-601 (1999).
